title: Practical Solutions to Common TAVI Complications
authors: Herbert Kroon
abstract: Aortic valve stenosis Calcific aortic valve degeneration mainly affects the elderly population. Approximately 15% of elderly patients have some degree of aortic stenosis (AS)1. Untreated severe AS will lead to heart failure, angina and/or syncope and approximately half of patients will expire within 2 years after symptom onset1, 2. Historically, open heart surgery was the only treatment for severe AS. However, advanced age was a dominant argument to defer surgery. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) was contrived as a less invasive alternative to surgery and to fulfill this unmet clinical need. After the first-in-human procedure in 2002, TAVI matured into a guideline recommended treatment of symptomatic severe AS in elderly patients across the entire risk spectrum3-7. Peri-procedural embolization Operator experience, improved planning and implantation strategies and multiple device iterations including smaller profile, repositioning ability and outer sealing fabric converted TAVI into a reproducible and relatively safe procedure8. However, the “Big Five” of complications in the modern TAVI era remain 1) access site complications and bleedings, 2) paravalvular leakage (PVL), 3) acute kidney injury (AKI), 4) conduction disturbances including the need for permanent pacemaker implantation (PPI) and 5) stroke9. Up to 5% of patients suffer a neurological event after TAVI, mainly within the first 48 hours8, 10, 11. This finding suggests a direct causative role with the transcatheter valve implantation itself. Transcranial Doppler and brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) studies revealed debris embolization towards the brain and new brain lesions after TAVI in the vast majority of patients12-15. Most of these embolizations remain clinically silent at first sight but may be linked to neurocognitive decline and frank dementia16. Embolic protection devices (EPD) have been developed to deflect or capture embolized debris on its way to the brain and may possibly reduce brain lesions and neurological events including stroke and neurocognitive decline. Part I of this thesis adds perspective to the etiopathology of TAVI related stroke and the mechanism of action of the current spectrum of cerebral embolic protection devices. We also present insights into the microscopic analysis of debris that was captured with filters during TAVI procedures. Vascular access and complications 1 TAVI typically requires large bore femoral artery access. By default, larger arteriotomies are at higher risk for access site complications and bleedings. A completely percutaneous approach relies on vascular access closure devices (VCD) to manage the arteriotomy and provide patent hemostasis. TAVI in low to intermediate risk patients is associated with a major vascular complication rate ranging between 2 and 8%4, 11. The conventional closure technique is based on sutures and most access site complications after TAVI procedures are related to closure device failure17. A collagen plug based closure device was introduced as an alternative to sutures. Part II of this thesis addresses vascular complications and provides information on clinical outcomes with collagen plug-based VCD. TAVI-related conduction disturbances Acquired conduction disturbances after TAVI are frequent and may lead to heart failure (re-) admissions and impaired long-term prognosis18-22. The atrioventricular bundle pierces the membranous septum between the right and non-coronary cusp of the aortic valve and surfaces along the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT), which makes it vulnerable to contact pressure by the implanted transcatheter heart valve (THV) during TAVI23, 24. New left bundle branch block (LBBB) and third-degree atrioventricular block (AV3B) requiring PPI occur in up to a third and quarter of patients, respectively18-22. These conduction disturbances may be transient or remain permanent which is clinically relevant in view of in-hospital stay and overall healthcare costs. Unfortunately, there are no uniform definitions to describe conduction dynamics post-TAVI. Inconsistent reporting makes the interpretation of the literature on this topic challenging. Part III of this thesis will elaborate on what is currently known about the incidence of newly acquired conduction disturbances after TAVI and studies specific features on the baseline and postprocedural electrocardiogram (ECG) to predict conduction dynamics. These insights may help determine the need and timing of PPI and adjust hospital discharge policies.

title: Evaluación de las posibles complicaciones pre y post implante percutáneo. Prótesis aórtica transcatéter
authors: Yolanda Bartolomé Fernández; Salvador Encinas Jiménez; Anna Penalva Domene; Gina Pi Iborra; Icar Tribó Miro

abstract: El implante valvular aórtico transcatéter constituye una alternativa terapéutica para pacientes con estenosis aórtica grave sintomática que presentan elevado riesgo quirúrgico o no son candidatos a cirugía convencional. La actuación enfermera resulta fundamental para la identificación precoz de necesidades y posibles complicaciones asociadas al procedimiento.

title: The Impact of Clinical and Biochemical Frailty on Outcomes following Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement
authors: Anant D. Butala; Joseph Hogarty; Shane Nanayakkara; Jason Bloom; Sonny C. Palmer; Samer Q. Noaman; David McGaw; David I. Blusztein; Rozanne Johnston; Ellen Gardner; Elisha Gartner; Jillian Pedetti; Nay Htun; David M. Kaye; Antony S. Walton; Dion A. Stub
abstract: BACKGROUND: Frailty results from declining reserve and function and is a modifiable cardiovascular risk-factor. Despite this, there is limited evidence surrounding its role in lower-risk TAVR cohorts. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to evaluate frailty among contemporary TAVR patients, delineate the impact of biochemical and clinical frailty, and understand its additive value to existing risk-prediction tools. METHODS: Analysis of a multicenter Australian registry. Biochemical frailty (BF) was defined as serum albumin <35 g/L and clinical frailty (CF) as a Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale ≥5. Patients meeting BF or CF criteria were categorized as frail. RESULTS: Of the 2,661 patients, the median age 82 (IQR: 77-86), 60% male, and median STS 3.3 (2-5.2), 920 patients (35%) were considered frail. A total of 171 (19%) of frail patients fulfilled both BF and CF criteria. The frail group was older (83 vs 81, P < 0.001), more females (43% vs 38%; P = 0.016) with higher STS scores (4 vs 3, P < 0.001). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed a stepwise increase in 12-month mortality with increasing frailty (no frailty 4% vs BF or CF 7% vs BF + CF 16%, Log-rank P < 0.001). In Cox proportional hazards regression BF or CF (adjusted HR: 1.6; 95% CI: 1.0-2.4; P = 0.033) and BF + CF (adjusted HR: 3.3; 95% CI: 1.9-5.6; P < 0.001) independently predicted 12-month mortality. Addition of frailty to STS Score improved mortality prediction (area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve: 0.608 vs 0.664; DeLong's P = 0.021), with Shapley analysis demonstrating significant contribution from frailty. CONCLUSIONS: Frailty is common with significant implications in TAVR. Patients with biochemical and clinical frailty criteria are highest risk. Development of strategies to address frailty is critical.

title: Triglyceride-glucose index and the incidence of peripheral artery disease: a dose-response meta-analysis of longitudinal studies
authors: Mofan Fu; Hucheng Teng; Zhen Li; Yuanshun Jiang; Baohua Sun
abstract: Background The triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index is a simple surrogate marker of insulin resistance and has been increasingly investigated as a predictor of cardiovascular diseases. However, longitudinal evidence regarding its association with incident peripheral artery disease (PAD) remains limited and inconsistent. We conducted a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis to evaluate the association between the TyG index and the risk of incident PAD. Methods PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science were systematically searched from inception to June 28, 2026. Longitudinal observational studies evaluating the association between the conventional TyG index and incidents PAD in adults were eligible. Pooled risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) comparing the highest versus lowest TyG categories were calculated using restricted maximum likelihood random-effects models. Linear and nonlinear dose-response meta-analyses were performed using restricted cubic spline models. Results Five longitudinal studies involving 417,499 participants and 7,800 incident PAD events were included. Compared with the lowest TyG category, a high TyG index was associated with a significantly increased risk of incident PAD (RR = 1.49, 95% CI 1.06 to 2.10; p = 0.02), although substantial heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 88.4%). Sensitivity analyses demonstrated robust findings. In the linear dose-response meta-analysis, each 1-unit increase in the TyG index was associated with a 22% higher risk of incident PAD (RR = 1.22, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.37; p = 0.001). Restricted cubic spline analysis demonstrated a significant overall dose-response association ( p = 0.001) with no evidence of nonlinearity ( p for nonlinearity = 0.367), indicating an approximately linear relationship between the TyG index and PAD risk. Conclusions A higher TyG index is associated with an increased risk of incident PAD in a dose-dependent and approximately linear manner. Systematic Review Registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/ , identifier CRD420261470450.

title: Prosthetic Heart Valve Orifice Area Detection By Using A Combined Shock-Anisotropic Coherence Filter To Improve Level Sets Algorithm
authors: Khalid Al-hammuri
abstract: Abstract Prosthetic valve is a synthetic or tissue substitute for the natural valve. It is designed to mimic the natural valve’s normal opening and clos-ing motions. The need for replacing heart valves increased drastically as the heart valve diseases became one of the dangerous death cause in the world. “Global demand for prosthetic heart valve market expected to reach USD 5,302.1 million in 2021 and growing of 9% from 2016 to 2021”. Unfortunately, Biological valves tend to fail over time, requir-ing replacement in 30% of patients within 10 years and 50% within 15 years. The demands for testing prosthetic valves are crucial to main-tain a robustness, durability and compatibility to improve patient health care which insure a place in the global market. This article discuss a novel method for automatic detection of a leaflet edges around ori-fice area opening for PHV (Prosthetic Heart Valve). A pre-processing algorithm using a combination of Anisotropic and Shock filter is proposed to enhance image quality before using a level set to detect PHV edges. This technique shows great capabilities to detect leaflet edges and provide additional enhancement compared to the other works.

title: Cardiac MRI-derived extracellular volume fraction is associated with failed left ventricular reverse remodeling after aortic valve replacement in severe aortic regurgitation With a giant left ventricle
authors: Hao Niu; Yangbo Yan; Xiangfeng Gong; Xiao Xiao; Changping Gan; ZhengHua Xiao
abstract: Severe chronic aortic regurgitation (AR) with a markedly dilated left ventricle (LV) (‘giant left ventricle’; LV end-diastolic diameter, LVEDD ≥65 mm) carries a high risk of incomplete LV reverse remodeling after aortic valve replacement (AVR), yet reliable preoperative stratification tools remain limited. This retrospective cohort study aimed to evaluate whether preoperative cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR)-derived extracellular volume fraction (ECV) is associated with 6-month LV reverse remodeling in this high-risk population. We enrolled 46 consecutive patients with severe AR and LVEDD ≥65 mm receiving contrast-enhanced CMR and elective AVR. The primary analysis assessed the association between preoperative ECV and the continuous relative change in LVEDD at 6 months; a binary definition (≥20% LVEDD reduction) was used as a secondary, clinically oriented outcome. Absence of significant LV reverse remodeling (<20% reduction) was observed in 47.8% (22/46) of patients. In linear regression analysis, higher preoperative ECV was significantly associated with a smaller LVEDD reduction ( β = −0.924 per 1% absolute increase in ECV, 95% CI −1.528 to −0.320, P = 0.004). In multivariable logistic regression restricted to the preoperative variables significant on univariable analysis (ECV and LVEDD), ECV remained associated with failed reverse remodeling (adjusted OR = 1.281 per 1% absolute increase in ECV, 95% CI 1.001–1.640, P = 0.049), although the association attenuated after further adjustment for age (OR 1.227, 95% CI 0.950–1.585, P = 0.117); with an exploratory cutoff of 34.1% (AUC=0.74, 95%CI 0.59–0.89). Patients with ECV >34.1% exhibited impaired postoperative LV systolic function and prolonged hospital stay. These exploratory findings suggest that preoperative CMR-ECV may help identify severe AR patients at risk of incomplete LV reverse remodeling after AVR, and warrant prospective validation.

title: Pattern of Congenital Heart Disease among Children Admitted to a Tertiary Care Hospital in Cumilla: A Hospital-Based Study
authors: Md Javed Iqbal; Md Shariful Haque; Khondaker Mobasher Ahmed; Md Mozibur Rahman; Mohammad Abdus Salam Molla; Tamanna Aftab Solaiman
journal: Journal of Comilla Medical College Teachers Association
abstract: Background: Congenital heart disease is the most common congenital problem in children. It causes significant childhood morbidity and mortality which could be reduced by early detection and proper management. Objectives: The objective of the study was to see the clinical & echocardiographic pattern of congenital heart disease among the hospital admitted children of a tertiary care hospital in Cumilla at present situation. Methods: This cross sectional observational study was done at Comilla Medical College Hospital from April 2024 to March 2025 among 100 patient with CHD who were diagnosed by color Doppler echocardiography aging from 1st day of life. Results: Acyanotic CHD was the most common CHD. VSD was the commonest acyanotic CHD (38%) followed by ASD (33%) & PDA (14%). Commonest cyanotic CHD was Tetralogy of Fallots (TOF) (4%) followed by TGA (2%). Male outnumbers female child. Most of the patients were diagnosed during infancy (59%). Common sign symptoms were respiratory distress (90%) cough (77%), fever (65%), cyanosis (41%), recurrent chest infection (70%) and murmur with or without thrill (60%). Conclusion: Ventricular septal defect (VSD) was the most common acyanotic CHD while Tetralogy of Follot (TOF) was the most frequent cyanotic CHD in this study. We hope that the result of this study will provide a database for future investigation on the pattern/distribution of CHD in tertiary hospital and raise the awareness about the significance of their early detection and surgical interventions. J Com Med Col Teachers’ Asso July 2026; 30(2): 88-92

title: Severe rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury associated with probable Legionella pneumophila infection: a case report
authors: Willis Thompson; Andrew John Mallett; Vikas Srivastava; John Di Giusto
abstract: Abstract Background Legionella pneumophila infection is an uncommon but recognised association with severe rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury. We describe an atypical, predominantly extrapulmonary presentation complicated by several plausible causes of rhabdomyolysis and update the literature since the 2020 systematic review. Case presentation A 78-year-old Caucasian male presented with three weeks of progressive lower-limb weakness, anorexia, weight loss, dark urine, oliguria, and a preceding flu-like illness. Examination demonstrated volume depletion and proximal lower-limb weakness with preserved upper-limb strength. Initial investigations revealed severe acute kidney injury, with creatinine 989 µmol/L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 4 mL/min/1.73 m², urea 40.2 mmol/L, and creatine kinase 33,400 U/L. Despite supportive treatment, progressive oliguria, metabolic acidosis, and hyperkalaemia necessitated haemodialysis. Investigations did not support autoimmune, obstructive or haematological causes; medication-related myotoxicity and metal-ion exposure remained possible. Legionella urinary antigen testing was negative. However, serology demonstrated L. pneumophila serogroup 1 IgM and total antibody titres ≥ 1:512. Without respiratory culture, PCR or paired serology, the findings supported probable recent infection rather than microbiologically proven Legionnaires’ disease. Conclusions This case demonstrates the diagnostic complexity of severe rhabdomyolysis-associated acute kidney injury when several plausible causes coexist. Probable recent Legionella infection was considered a potential precipitating factor. A negative urinary antigen result does not exclude Legionella infection when clinical and epidemiological suspicion persists, although single-titre serology should be interpreted cautiously.

title: ICP en candidatos a TAVI con enfermedad coronaria: impacto de la estrategia y el momento de la revascularizaci�n en el pron�stico
authors: Ricardo Micael Mendes Morais Carvalheiro; Miguel Marques Antunes; Francisco Barbas de Albuquerque; Bárbara Teixeira; A Grazina; Pedro Brás; Tiago Mendonça; Luis Almeida Morais; Inês Rodrigues; Tiago Pereira da Silva; Rúben Ramos; António José Fiarresga; Rui Cruz Ferreira; Duarte Cacela
abstract: Introducción y objetivos: La coronariopatía es frecuente en candidatos a implante percutáneo de válvula aórtica (TAVI), pero el beneficio y el momento óptimo de la intervención coronaria percutánea (ICP) perioperatoria siguen siendo inciertos.Se evaluaron el impacto pronóstico y el momento de la ICP perioperatoria en candidatos a TAVI con coronariopatía significativa.Métodos: Estudio retrospectivo de pacientes con estenosis aórtica grave sintomática y coronariopatía significativa sometidos a TAVI en un centro terciario portugués (2009-2023).Los pacientes recibieron ICP perioperatoria planificada (≤ 6 meses antes del TAVI o concomitante con este) o tratamiento médico.Los objetivos principales fueron las supervivencias global y cardiovascular a 24 meses.Los objetivos secundarios incluyeron la mortalidad a 30 días, los eventos cardiovasculares adversos mayores (MACE), las hemorragias potencialmente mortales, los cambios analíticos perioperatorios y la revascularización no planificada.Se aplicó emparejamiento por puntuación de propensión.También se comparó el momento de la ICP (antes del TAVI frente a concomitante con este).Resultados: De los 174 pacientes, 80 (46,0%) recibieron ICP y 94 (54,0%) tratamiento médico.A los 24 meses, las supervivencias global y cardiovascular fueron comparables (19,5 frente a 18,2 meses; p = 0,586; y 22,3 frente a 20,8 meses; p = 0,182, respectivamente).En la cohorte emparejada (n = 108), la ICP no mostró un beneficio en términos de supervivencia (mortalidad por cualquier causa: HR = 0,98; p = 0,950; cardiovascular: HR = 1,40; p = 0,610).No se observaron diferencias en la mortalidad a 30 días, los MACE, las hemorragias ni la revascularización.La ICP concomitante requirió un mayor volumen de contraste y procedimientos más prolongados; el análisis no ajustado sugirió menor supervivencia a 24 meses, pero esta asociación no persistió tras el ajuste multivariable.Conclusiones: En candidatos a TAVI con coronariopatía obstructiva, la ICP perioperatoria planificada no mejoró la supervivencia frente al tratamiento médico.

title: Analysis and Identification of Risk Factors for Intradialytic Hypotension in Patients Undergoing Maintenance Hemodialysis
authors: Xiaolong Yin; Yanmei Li; Ting Zhang; Jianhua Ye
abstract: OBJECTIVE: This paper aimed to identify factors associated with intradialytic hypotension (IDH) in patients receiving maintenance hemodialysis (MHD) and to develop a practical risk prediction model for early clinical assessment. METHODS: A retrospective analysis included 142 patients on MHD, divided into an IDH group (n = 48) and a non-IDH group (n = 94) based on intradialytic systolic blood pressure decline and related clinical intervention. Blood pressure parameters, demographic characteristics, dialysis prescription, biochemical indicators, and bone mineral metabolism markers were collected. Independent risk factors for IDH were identified via multivariate logistic regression of univariate significant variables, and a nomogram was constructed based on regression coefficients. Model performance was assessed using the Hosmer-Lemeshow test, calibration curve, ROC analysis, and bootstrap internal validation. RESULTS: Patients with IDH showed lower intradialytic SBP/DBP and greater blood pressure reduction than those without IDH (p < 0.05). Older age, higher dry weight (DW), transferrin saturation, and parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels were associated with IDH in univariate analysis (p < 0.05). Multivariate analysis confirmed age (OR = 1.059), DW (OR = 1.043), and PTH (OR = 1.001) as independent risk factors (p < 0.05). Based on these three factors, the constructed nomogram model showed good calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow test p = 0.249), with an AUC of 0.750 (95% CI 0.674-0.837), and an internally validated corrected C-index of 0.740 (95% CI 0.662-0.825). CONCLUSION: Advanced age, increased DW, and elevated PTH are significant predictors of IDH in MHD patients. The nomogram provides a reliable tool for individualized early warning and risk evaluation.

title: How do regional blood flow rates measured by arterial Doppler vary during hemorrhagic shock? An experimental study in anesthetized piglets
authors: Colin Azria; Céline Occelli; Edwin Bodet; Thomas Sanchez; Thibaut Markarian; Florian Ajavon; Marylène Bacle; Xavier Bobbia; Fabien Coisy
abstract: Abstract Hemorrhagic shock induces compensatory vasoconstriction that may affect arterial territories differently. Regional blood flow (RBF) can be assessed using Doppler ultrasound with the time-averaged mean velocity (TAMV). The primary objective was to describe changes in RBF among the carotid, femoral, superior mesenteric and renal arterial territories across blood depletion during controlled hemorrhagic shock in anesthetized piglets. Anesthetized and mechanically ventilated piglets underwent controlled blood withdrawal at 2 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ until a mean arterial pressure of 40 mmHg was reached. At baseline and after each 5-mL·kg⁻¹ depletion step, VTI was measured in the carotid, femoral, superior mesenteric and renal arteries. TAMV was calculated as VTI × HR / 60 and normalized to each animal’s baseline value. TAMV was analyzed using linear mixed-effects models with a subject-specific random intercept. Fixed effects were assessed using type III analysis of variance and reported as F statistics with Satterthwaite-approximated degrees of freedom. Pairwise comparisons were adjusted for multiple testing by Holm method. Seventeen piglets were analyzed, with a median blood withdrawal of 38 [34; 42] mL·kg⁻¹. Median carotid, femoral, renal and mesenteric TAMV values and their interquartile ranges were 16 [14; 20], 23 [15; 29], 26 [19; 42] and 55 [40; 66] cm·s⁻¹ at T0; 19 [15; 24], 25 [19; 38], 25 [17; 30] and 44 [36; 53] cm·s⁻¹ at 10 mL·kg⁻¹; 17 [14; 24], 26 [22; 40], 26 [18; 34] and 41 [38; 48] cm·s⁻¹ at 20 mL·kg⁻¹; 21 [16; 22], 25 [19; 32], 23 [19; 31] and 41 [36; 51] cm·s⁻¹ at 30 mL·kg⁻¹; and 20 [17; 22], 27 [25; 30], 16 [14; 16] and 48 [39; 59] cm·s⁻¹ at 40 mL·kg⁻¹, respectively. Overall territorial comparisons were F (3, 109) = 17.14 ( p < 0.01) at T0 and F (3, 109) = 18.92 ( p < 0.01) at T1. Within-territory analyses were F (8, 93) = 1.69 (Holm-adjusted p = 0.34) for the carotid territory, F (8, 91) = 2.10 (Holm-adjusted p = 0.18) for the femoral territory, F (8, 76) = 1.02 (Holm-adjusted p = 0.43) for the mesenteric territory, and F (8, 96) = 1.55 (Holm-adjusted p = 0.34) for the renal territory. The depletion step-by-territory interaction was F (24, 393) = 0.85 ( p = 0.68). The variations in RBF assessed by Doppler appeared to be heterogeneous across different territories, with carotid blood flow remaining preserved, although the study’s statistical power was insufficient to confirm this difference.

title: Absent vestibular evoked myogenic potentials and graviception cofactors in adults with diabetes
authors: Kathrine Jáuregui‐Renaud; José Adán Miguel‐Puga; Aida García-López; María de Lourdes Tirado-Mondragón; Lourdes Guadalupe González-Carrasco
abstract: This study was designed to explore the clinical characteristics (including quadriceps strength) of 166 adults (28–80 years old) with diabetes who have either present or absent bilateral otolith reflex responses by Vestibular Evoked Myogenic Potentials (VEMPs), and its relation to graviception by the Subjective Visual Vertical (S.V.V.). After retinoscopy, electromyography, audiology, vestibular function and quadriceps strength evaluations, assessments were performed on ocular and cervical VEMPs, and estimation of S.V.V., during static condition and on-axis/ off-axis rotation (utricle/ semicircular canal stimulation). 43.9% participants had absent ocular VEMPs, which were not related to on-axis/ off-axis estimations, but to the quadriceps strength; 5.4% participants had absent cervical VEMPs. The S.V.V. during on-axis and off-axis rotation showed no linear relation to present/absent VEMPs, but to static S.V.V. standard deviation (precision), and to an interaction among gender, high blood pressure and dyslipidemia. In conclusion, in adults with diabetes, metabolic compromise and macrovascular factors might contribute to otolith dysfunction; while the presence/absence of ocular VEMPs can be dissociated from the presence/absence of cervical VEMPs and from graviception during utricle/semicircular canal stimulation.

title: Prognostic value of native T1 mapping and extracellular volume fraction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: A systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Qi Wang; Wenqi Liu; Jingjing Shi; Wanzhen Li; Jie Lin; Zhenchang Wang; Yiyuan Gao
abstract: Background Accurate risk stratification in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) remains challenging, and the prognostic significance of cardiovascular magnetic resonance-derived native T1 mapping and extracellular volume fraction (ECV) remains uncertain. Aims To systematically evaluate the prognostic value of native T1 mapping and ECV in HCM patients. Methods PubMed, Embase, MEDLINE, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to February 6, 2026. Eligible studies assessed native T1 and/or ECV for prognosis in HCM. Baseline values, mean differences, and hazard ratios (HRs) were synthesized using random-effects models. Effect estimates were standardized as HRs per 30-ms increase in native T1 and per 1% increase in ECV. Results Eight longitudinal cohort studies involving 2539 HCM patients were included. Elevated native T1 was significantly associated with an increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) (HR=1.27, 95% CI: 1.12–1.44, P < 0.001), as was higher ECV (HR=1.10, 95% CI: 1.07–1.14, P < 0.001). For sudden cardiac death-related outcomes, the association with native T1 was not significant, whereas elevated ECV was associated with an increased risk (HR=1.14, 95% CI: 1.01–1.28, P = 0.04), although substantial heterogeneity was observed and sensitivity analysis indicated limited robustness (HR=1.05, 95% CI: 0.97–1.14, P = 0.21). For heart failure-related outcomes, only ECV was associated with risk (HR=1.10, 95% CI: 1.05–1.15; P < 0.001). Conclusions Native T1 and ECV were associated with MACE risk in HCM, and ECV was additionally associated with heart failure-related outcomes. Their value for sudden cardiac death-related risk prediction requires further validation. PROSPERO registration number CRD420261406609

title: Effect of zinc histidine hydrate in maintenance hemodialysis patients with hypozincemia
authors: Shigeru Otsubo; Sho Okano; Miwa Bando; Naoko Miwa; Takao Kubota
abstract: Abstract Background Zinc is an essential trace element involved in numerous physiological processes, including immune function, wound healing, and protein synthesis. Hypozincemia is common in patients undergoing maintenance hemodialysis; however, evidence regarding the clinical effects of zinc supplementation in this population remains limited. This study aimed to investigate the prevalence of hypozincemia and evaluate the effects of zinc histidine hydrate. Methods We retrospectively analyzed clinical data from 269 patients undergoing maintenance hemodialysis at three facilities. Associations between serum zinc concentrations and other laboratory parameters were assessed. In addition, changes in laboratory parameters were evaluated in 53 patients who received zinc histidine hydrate for 3 months. Results The mean serum zinc concentration was 70 ± 18 µg/dL. Serum zinc concentrations were below 80 µg/dL in 81.8% of patients. After 3 months of treatment, serum zinc concentrations increased significantly from 58 ± 9 to 96 ± 37 µg/dL (P < 0.001). Serum alkaline phosphatase concentrations also increased significantly, from 79 ± 37 to 87 ± 44 U/L (P = 0.004). Serum copper concentrations decreased significantly from 95 ± 18 to 86 ± 22 µg/dL (P < 0.001). One of the 54 patients who initiated treatment discontinued it because of nausea. Conclusions Hypozincemia was prevalent among patients undergoing maintenance hemodialysis. Zinc histidine hydrate treatment was associated with increased serum zinc and alkaline phosphatase concentrations and decreased serum copper concentrations. Monitoring serum copper during treatment is important.

title: Mid-term outcomes of right atrial appendage–derived pulmonary valve reconstruction during transannular repair of tetralogy of Fallot
authors: Ahmet Kuddusi İrdem; Onur Doyurgan
abstract: Objectives Transannular patch (TAP) repair remains necessary when pulmonary annular preservation is not feasible during tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) repair, but the resulting pulmonary regurgitation (PR) may contribute to progressive right ventricular volume loading and late reintervention. We evaluated early and mid-term outcomes of right atrial appendage (RAA)-derived bicuspid pulmonary valve reconstruction compared with monocusp and valve-free TAP reconstruction. Methods We conducted a two-center retrospective comparative cohort study of 49 patients undergoing TOF repair requiring transannular RVOT reconstruction by a single surgeon. Twenty-two patients underwent RAA-derived bicuspid pulmonary valve reconstruction, 14 underwent monocusp TAP reconstruction, and 13 underwent valve-free TAP reconstruction. The three reconstruction strategies were analyzed separately, with an additional RAA-versus-monocusp sensitivity comparison. Because age at repair differed among groups, an additional sensitivity analysis for the principal echocardiographic outcome was restricted to the overlapping age range of the RAA and monocusp groups. Results Median follow-up was 31.5 months (IQR, 28.0–36.0) after RAA reconstruction, 25.5 months (23.0–34.5) after monocusp TAP, and 30.0 months (26.0–36.0) after valve-free TAP ( p = 0.224). At the last available follow-up echocardiographic examination, moderate/severe PR was present in 1 of 22 patients (4.5%) after RAA reconstruction, 13 of 14 (92.9%) after monocusp TAP, and 13 of 13 (100%) after valve-free TAP ( p < 0.001). The association persisted in the direct RAA-versus-monocusp comparison (4.5% vs. 92.9%; risk ratio, 0.05; 95% CI, 0.01–0.33; Fisher's exact p < 0.001) and in the age-restricted sensitivity analysis [1/16 [6.3%] vs. 9/10 [90.0%]; Fisher's exact p < 0.001]. No patient in the RAA or monocusp group underwent pulmonary valve replacement (PVR), whereas three patients in the valve-free TAP group underwent PVR during subsequent clinical follow-up. Conclusions RAA-derived bicuspid pulmonary valve reconstruction was feasible and was associated with a lower prevalence of moderate/severe PR during mid-term follow-up compared with both monocusp and valve-free TAP reconstruction in this retrospective cohort. The association persisted after exclusion of the valve-free TAP group and in an age-restricted sensitivity analysis. These findings warrant confirmation in larger prospective studies with standardized longitudinal imaging and longer follow-up before conclusions regarding long-term durability, right ventricular remodeling, or PVR risk can be established.

title: Beyond Structured Vitals: Semantic-Temporal Alignment for Full-Record ICU Risk Forecasting
authors: Zhichong Zheng; Xiaohang Nie; Xueqi Wang; Yuanjin Zhao; Haitao Zhang; Yichao Tang
journal: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
abstract: Traditional Electronic Health Record (EHR) datasets heavily favor structured data, often missing the nuanced progression of patients in intensive care. To address this gap, we introduce FRICU, a newly constructed dataset integrating structured vitals with full-record clinical narratives across complete admission trajectories using expert-verified, event-level annotations. Recognizing that the pathological impact of historical events depends on their semantic content rather than mere chronological proximity, we propose Semantic-Temporal Alignment (SeTA), a semantic-guided temporal attention mechanism that dynamically calibrates temporal receptive fields for query-specific evidence retrieval. For supervision, expert-verified risk labels are transformed into continuous trajectories via bidirectional Gaussian decay, providing smooth event-level supervision for gradual risk evolution. On FRICU, SeTA achieves a Sample AUPRC of 0.428, improving over TALE-EHR by 21.2%. On MIMIC-IV, SeTA achieves the best AUPRC on IMV and mortality prediction and remains competitive on sepsis prediction, demonstrating generalization beyond text-intensive full-record trajectories. To facilitate reproducibility, our code is available at https://github.com/violetesk/SeTA-FRICU.

title: Evaluation of risk factors for tricuspid regurgitation prior to cardiac pacemaker
authors: Shuangling Wang; Qiuzhe Guo; Li Li; Guochun Li; Ying Zhou; Yunfei Zhou; Guodong Niu; Yulong Guo
abstract: Objective To identify factors associated with preprocedural tricuspid regurgitation (TR) in patients with bradyarrhythmia undergoing cardiac pacemaker implantation and to evaluate the impact of preprocedural TR severity on postprocedural TR evolution and clinical outcomes. Methods This retrospective study included 767 patients with bradyarrhythmia who underwent permanent pacemaker implantation at Fuwai Yunnan Cardiovascular Hospital between January 2020 and October 2024. Patients were stratified into four groups according to preprocedural TR severity: none, mild, moderate, and severe. Clinical data, laboratory parameters, and echocardiographic parameters were collected. Univariate analysis was used to compare differences among groups, and ordinal logistic regression was used to identify independent factors associated with preprocedural TR. Among the 501 patients with follow-up of at least 2 months, binary logistic regression was used to evaluate the impact of preprocedural TR on postprocedural outcomes. Results Multivariable analysis showed that female sex (OR = 1.573), heart failure (OR = 1.837), persistent atrial fibrillation (OR = 4.958), and pulmonary hypertension (OR = 6.586) were independent risk factors for greater preprocedural TR severity, whereas higher BMI (OR = 0.920) was an independent protective factor (all P < 0.05). At a median follow-up of 16 months after pacemaker implantation, greater preprocedural TR severity was associated with more frequent postprocedural rehospitalizations ( P = 0.007) and a higher risk of cardiac function deterioration ( P < 0.001). Compared with patients without preprocedural TR, those with moderate or severe preprocedural TR had a significantly lower risk of postprocedural TR worsening and a higher rate of TR improvement, with this benefit being more pronounced in younger patients. Conclusions In patients with bradyarrhythmia undergoing cardiac pacing, preprocedural TR severity is influenced by multiple factors, including sex, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and pulmonary hypertension. Greater preprocedural TR severity is associated with worse postprocedural cardiac functional outcomes. Among patients with pre-existing moderate-to-severe TR, a substantial proportion show improvement in TR after pacemaker implantation, and younger patients are more likely to benefit from such improvement. Cardiac pacing does not exert exclusively detrimental effects on TR.

title: Ultrasound-based assessment of cardiac and hepatic dysfunction: current status and future directions
authors: Yin-Xia Li; Lei Chen; Peng Chen; Yi-Sheng Wang; Rui Shen
abstract: Heart failure (HF) is a systemic syndrome in which venous congestion and impaired perfusion can produce clinically important hepatic dysfunction. The term cardiohepatic syndrome (CHS) describes this bidirectional interaction, but cardiac and hepatic abnormalities are still often evaluated in parallel rather than as a connected hemodynamic process. Ultrasound is uniquely suited to an integrated assessment because it can characterize cardiac structure and function, systemic venous congestion, hepatic hemodynamics, tissue stiffness, and treatment-related change at the bedside. Conventional transthoracic echocardiography remains the foundation of evaluation, while three-dimensional echocardiography and speckle-tracking techniques improve quantification of right ventricular, atrial, and subclinical myocardial dysfunction. Abdominal Doppler ultrasound, venous congestion scoring, and liver elastography add complementary information, although liver stiffness must be interpreted cautiously because congestion, inflammation, cholestasis, and fibrosis can produce overlapping signals. Artificial intelligence may improve acquisition, measurement reproducibility, and multimodal data integration, but external validation and transparent reporting remain essential. This review summarizes contemporary evidence and proposes a practical, sequential pathway that combines echocardiography, venous Doppler findings, liver stiffness, laboratory biomarkers, and dynamic reassessment after decongestion. The central clinical principle is that CHS should be evaluated as a time-varying cardiohepatic phenotype rather than diagnosed from a single cardiac, hepatic, or biochemical measurement. Integrated ultrasound assessment of cardiohepatic syndrome. Heart failure produces a continuum from myocardial dysfunction and elevated filling pressures to systemic venous congestion, hepatic sinusoidal stress, and potentially fibrosis. A combined protocol uses echocardiography to define the cardiac substrate, venous Doppler ultrasound to quantify pressure transmission, and liver elastography plus biomarkers to characterize hepatic injury. Dynamic reassessment after decongestion helps distinguish reversible congestion from persistent structural liver disease and supports risk-adapted management.

title: Challenges and innovations in cardiac AAV gene delivery as a platform for cardiac regeneration
authors: Gabriella Kabboul; Alejandro Izurieta Muñoz; Muath M. Bishawi; Christopher B. Doering; Rebecca D. Levit
abstract: Gene therapies are at the forefront of potential treatments for cardiovascular diseases, but clinical translation remains limited by poor myocardial access and retention, systemic distribution, and immune-mediated toxicities. Heavily underexplored, the route of administration dictates efficacy and safety, ultimately influencing therapeutic outcomes. This review addresses the role of delivery in overcoming these challenges in cardiac adeno-associated viral therapies. Emphasis is placed on biomaterial-based delivery approaches to improve therapeutic outcomes.

title: Physiological markers of low-altitude exercise load for predicting acute mountain sickness: development of an interpretable machine learning model and research web calculator
authors: Fengbo Miao; Yi Yuan; Shuai Wang; Chengli Tao; Yupeng Liu; Qi Mao; Hualin Zhang; Ning Li; Renzheng Chen; Jianfu Sui
abstract: Acute mountain sickness (AMS) poses a significant threat to individuals ascending to high-altitude regions, yet early identification of susceptible populations remains challenging. This study aimed to develop an interpretable machine learning model for estimating AMS risk from exercise-induced physiological responses measured at low altitude. A total of 171 healthy participants were included, with 111 participants (51 AMS events) comprising the development cohort and 60 participants (27 AMS events) forming an external validation cohort. Model development was repeated within a nested cross-validation framework, including LASSO feature selection and algorithm selection within the resampling process. The final locked five-feature model included changes in post-exercise pulse oxygen saturation (ΔSpO 2 ) and cardiac output (ΔCO), sex, smoking history, and drinking history, and combined logistic regression, support vector machine, and random forest by equal-weight soft voting. In the development cohort, pooled outer-fold predictions yielded an AUC of 0.866 (95% CI, 0.791–0.929), an AUPRC of 0.842 (95% CI, 0.748–0.932), and a Brier score of 0.148. The calibration intercept was −0.033 (95% CI, −0.504 to 0.527), the calibration slope was 0.931 (95% CI, 0.664–1.351) and the positive net benefit range was 0.078–0.840. In the external validation cohort, the locked model yielded an AUC of 0.834 (95% CI, 0.723–0.929), an AUPRC of 0.867 (95% CI, 0.758–0.946), and a Brier score of 0.152; the calibration intercept was −0.103 (95% CI, −0.834 to 0.531), the calibration slope was 1.013 (95% CI, 0.655–1.666) and a positive net benefit range of 0.200–0.953. Post-hoc SHAP analysis identified ΔSpO 2 and ΔCO as the two most influential predictors. These findings support an association between low-altitude exercise responses and subsequent AMS. However, the prediction model requires further development and validation in substantially larger cohorts before clinical deployment.

title: Mechanosensing channels PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 regulate mitral valve serotonin-mediated homeostasis and pathophysiology
authors: Emily Hall
abstract: Mitral regurgitation (MR) pathophysiology involves increased serotonin (5-HT) receptor (HTR) expression and signalling, together with reduced 5-HT transporter (SLC6A4) expression in mitral valve interstitial cells (MVIC). The mechanosensitive calcium channels, PIEZO1 and PIEZO2, regulate cellular responses to a variety of mechanical conditions; however, PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 have not been studied in MR. We investigated the hypothesis that PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 mediate, through 5-HT mechanisms, both homeostasis in normal mitral valves (nMV) and in the pathophysiology of MR.

title: Systemic Laboratory Alterations Associated With Heart Failure in Severe Mitral Regurgitation: A Retrospective Observational Study
authors: Emilia Sorina Fiat; Nastaca Alina Palade; Crina Cristina Solomon; Razvan Constantin Vonica; Bogdan Ioan Vintilă; Maria Totan; Anca Maria Arseniu; Claudiu Morgovan; Anca Butucă; Adina Frum; Carmen Maximiliana Dobrea; Diter Atasie; Felicia Gabriela Gligor
abstract: Background: The systemic laboratory abnormalities accompanying documented heart failure in patients hospitalized with severe mitral regurgitation (MR) have not been fully characterized across multiple biological domains within the same cohort.Methodology: In this retrospective, single-center, cross-sectional study, 107 adults with echocardiographically documented severe MR were compared according to the presence (n = 49) or absence (n = 58) of a heart failure diagnosis at discharge.Inflammatory, hematological, renal, electrolyte, hepatic, and coagulation measures were evaluated using multiplicity-adjusted comparisons and age-and sexadjusted domain-specific logistic regression.A post hoc model integrating age, sex, C-reactive protein, anemia, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <60 mL/min/1.73m² was explored using sensitivity analyses and fixed-model bootstrap validation.Results: Multiple laboratory domains differed by heart failure status.In the post hoc integrated model, eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73m² showed the most consistent association with concomitant heart failure (odds ratio, 5.56; 95% confidence interval, 1.94-15.94;P = 0.001); C-reactive protein and anemia were not statistically significant after mutual adjustment.The apparent and optimism-corrected areas under the curve were 0.809 and 0.780, respectively; corresponding Brier scores were 0.175 and 0.196.Conclusions: Among hospitalized patients with severe MR, documented concomitant heart failure was accompanied by abnormalities across several laboratory domains, with reduced renal function showing the most consistent association in exploratory multivariable analyses.The retrospective design, dischargediagnosis-based heart failure classification, incomplete echocardiographic characterization, and limited sample size preclude causal or predictive interpretations.

title: May-Thurner Syndrome Presenting as Submassive Pulmonary Embolism in a Young Male: A Case Report
authors: Anita Ho; Colleen Chen; Suchith B Suresh; Omar Adeeb; Helen Stutz
abstract: May-Thurner syndrome (MTS) is an anatomic variant in which the right common iliac artery compresses the left common iliac vein, predisposing to left lower extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT).While MTS predominantly affects young women, we present a case of a 24-year-old African American male with a family history suggestive of hereditary hypercoagulability who developed a massive bilateral pulmonary embolism (PE) with right heart strain and extensive left lower extremity DVT, revealing underlying MTS as the anatomic substrate for his thrombotic event.Management included systemic anticoagulation, mechanical pulmonary thrombectomy, and percutaneous lower extremity thrombectomy, with plans for outpatient hypercoagulability evaluation.

title: Echocardiographic phenotypes of opioid-induced cardiotoxicity: a narrative review
authors: Krzysztof Żerdziński; Julita Janiec; Alexander Suchodolski; Mariola Szulik
abstract: Opioid cardiotoxicity is an increasing clinical concern, yet its echocardiographic manifestations are heterogeneous and poorly characterized. This narrative review synthesizes available evidence, maps the principal echocardiographic phenotypes of opioid-related cardiac injury, and identifies major knowledge gaps. A structured PubMed search (January 2014-December 2024) combined opioid and echocardiographic terms without language restriction. Human and animal studies of any design assessing cardiac structure or function by echocardiography after acute or chronic opioid exposure were eligible. Of 209 records, 41 were included and grouped by dominant phenotype. No formal protocol (e.g., PRISMA) or risk-of-bias appraisal was applied. Five distinct-and often conflicting-phenotypes emerged: (1) severe, potentially reversible global left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVEF as low as 20%), sometimes progressing to cardiogenic shock yet normalising within 48-72 h; (2) Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, classic after withdrawal and predominantly reverse after intoxication; (3) right ventricular dysfunction with pulmonary hypertension, usually secondary to hypoxia or left-sided failure but occasionally isolated; (4) consistent cardioprotection in animal ischaemia-reperfusion models, unsupported by any prospective human echocardiographic study; and (5) a mechanically normal profile despite QTc exceeding 610 ms and torsades de pointes. Phenotypes 1-3 rest largely on case reports, and many studies are confounded by co-administered cocaine, benzodiazepines or α2-adrenoceptor agonists. Opioid cardiac effects are context-dependent, and mechanical toxicity diverges from electrical toxicity: a normal echocardiogram does not exclude lethal arrhythmia, so echocardiography and serial QTc assessment are complementary rather than interchangeable. Prospective studies with advanced imaging are needed to establish phenotype frequency and determinants.

title: Differential hypoxaemia before aortic cross-clamping during minimally invasive mitral valve surgery: a case report
authors: Kübra Gözaçık Karakoç; Şahin Kapan; Veli Tackin; Nevzat Erdil
abstract: Differential hypoxaemia, also known as Harlequin syndrome or North–South syndrome, occurs during peripheral cardiopulmonary bypass when poorly oxygenated blood ejected by the native heart competes with retrograde oxygenated blood delivered from a femoral arterial cannula, so that the aortic arch vessels and the cerebral circulation may be perfused with deoxygenated blood. It is well described in venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation but is a less familiar complication of minimally invasive cardiac surgery. We report its occurrence before aortic cross-clamping during minimally invasive mitral valve surgery, whilst native ejection was presumed to persist and pulmonary ventilation had been suspended for surgical exposure. A 38-year-old man with rheumatic heart disease and severe mitral regurgitation (left ventricular ejection fraction 60%) underwent minimally invasive mitral valve surgery through a right anterior minithoracotomy with peripheral cardiopulmonary bypass established by femoral cannulation. Invasive arterial pressure was monitored from the right radial artery. Before aortic cross-clamping, whilst native ejection was presumed to persist, the blood visible in the aortic root vent line of the vented antegrade cardioplegia cannula appeared darker and the right-hand oxygen saturation fell to approximately 50%; arterial blood gas analysis showed a partial pressure of oxygen of 226 mmHg in the oxygenator outflow but only 23 mmHg in the right radial artery, confirming differential hypoxaemia. Two-lung ventilation was resumed, and the right-hand oxygen saturation recovered promptly. A 31-mm mechanical prosthesis was implanted and the patent foramen ovale was closed through the same incision. The patient was extubated 4 h postoperatively without clinically apparent neurological deficit and was discharged on postoperative day 5, remaining in New York Heart Association class I at five months. Differential hypoxaemia can complicate minimally invasive mitral valve surgery when antegrade native output persists. Right radial arterial monitoring provides a sentinel indicator of oxygenation in the brachiocephalic territory and allowed early recognition in this patient. Early restoration of pulmonary gas exchange may limit severe upper-body hypoxaemic exposure and potentially reduce neurological risk.

title: Interpretable AI for echocardiography-based early screening of rheumatic heart disease in Ethiopia: a cost-effective strategy to tackle a persistent global health disparity
authors: Daniel Moges Tadesse; Demeke Mekonnen; olyad mulugeta; Samuel Rahimeto Kebede; Fraol Gelana Waldamichael; Taye Girma Debelee; Hiwot Taye Mekonnen
abstract: Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) is a serious condition that develops from untreated streptococcal throat infections and causes long-term damage to the heart valves. Although it is become rare in wealthier countries, it still affects many people in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), like sub-Saharan Africa, where fragmented healthcare infrastructure and limited access to specialized diagnostics exacerbate diagnostic delays. This study presents an interpretable artificial intelligence (AI) framework designed to automate early RHD screening using echocardiographic imaging, with a focus on addressing critical diagnostic gaps in resource-constrained settings such as Ethiopia. Our study explores how Interpretable AI based approach can help identify early signs of RHD using echocardiographic images, primarily mitral regurgitation (MR). Specifically, we focus on detecting mitral regurgitation in two views (A​pical​ ​five chamber (AP5) and Parasternal long axis (PSLAX) views) during the heart’s systolic cycle and measuring the thickness of the anterior mitral valve leaflet (AMVL) from the PSLAX view as part of the old criteria. To do this, we trained and compared two AI models to segment the left atrium (LA) and mitral valve (MV) using annotated echocardiographic datasets. By tracking vol​ume changes in the segmented LA, we identified the frames corresponding to the systolic cycle. To detect MR, which is a key pathological hallmark of RHD, we then overlaid Color Doppler blood flow information on the segmented LA regions of the systolic frames. Additionally, the MV segmentation model was used to measure the AMVL thickness during systole, a critical morphological indicator of chronic valvular damage which was not part of our primary focus. Importantly, this AI framework was developed primarily for the detection of World Heart Federation (WHF) significant MR. While AMVL thickness was examined as an additional morphological parameter, its measurement was performed during sys​tole for methodological convenience and has not been validated for the assessment of mitral stenosis. Furthermore, the framework does not evaluate restricted mitral leaflet motion. Therefore, leaflet thickness measurements should be regarded as exploratory findings and not as diagnostic outputs of the proposed system. Trained on annotated echocardiographic datasets and tested on an independent pilot test set of real-world scans from Ethiopian regional hospitals (patients not seen during training or validation), the AI model demonstrated promis​ing results, achieving precision (1.0), recall (0.7), F1-score (0.82), and accuracy (0.7) metrics that underscore its potential for reliable deployment in low-resource environments. The system’s interpretable design, which visualizes segmentation boundaries, Doppler flow patterns, and anatomical measurements, prioritizes clinical transparency, enabling healthcare workers to validate AI outputs against familiar diagnostic benchmarks. By automating labor-intensive echocardiographic analyses, this AI-driven strat​egy could revolutionize early RHD detection in LMICs, reducing reliance on scarce specialist expertise and paving the way for scalable, cost-effective screening programs. Our findings highlight the transformative role of context-specific AI solutions in bridging global health inequities.

title: Pacing in adults with complex congenital heart disease: A narrative minireview
authors: Vasileios Papaioannou; Julia Jones; Fahmi Faraz; David Mayhew; Archana Rao; Matthew Kahn; Sarah Moharem Elgamal; Reza Ashrafi
abstract: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is a growing health care problem, as more pediatric patients survive to adulthood every year as the number of patients with complex conditions also increases.As more patients survive, there has been an increase in the need for pacemaker procedures.Historically, there has been a focus on epicardial pacing in the most complex groups.In this review, we examine the background epidemiology, existing evidence for pacing, extraction data in three of the most complex CHD groups-transposition of the great arteries with an atrial switch procedure, patients palliated with a Fontan procedure and univentricular hearts.In this expert narrative review, we have used a broad search strategy of PubMed supplemented with evidence where available from non-congenital cohorts.The evidence in these most complex cohorts can be limited to expert centre opinion, small numbers and mixed paediatric/adult data.We discuss below the available data, the limitations and the novel approaches available in centres to deal with the most complex conditions such as conduction system pacing and leadless pacing with promising results albeit in expert centres only.Whilst current applicability to a wider range of institutions is not yet suggested by the paper, this review hopefully illustrates potential options for consideration and research in the future.

title: Single-session transcatheter mitral repair and left atrial appendage occlusion: evidence and practical considerations
authors: Juan Gabriel Cordoba-Soriano; Jesús María Jiménez-Mazuecos; Juan Carlos García-López; Pablo Valentín-García; and Laura Guerra-Luján; Macarena López-Vázquez

title: Invasive Candida viswanathii infections in critically ill neonates: clinical challenges and management insights from a case series
authors: Domenico Umberto De Rose; Chiara Maddaloni; Ludovica Martini; Alessandra Santisi; Venere Cortazzo; Serena Raimondi; Gianluca Vrenna; Francesca Ippolita Calò Carducci; Laura Lancella; Irma Capolupo; Paola Bernaschi; Marta Luisa Ciofi degli Atti; Carlo Federico Perno; Andrea Dotta; Maria Paola Ronchetti; Massimiliano Raponi
abstract: Background Candida species continue to be a major cause of invasive fungal infections in neonatal intensive care units, with a growing awareness of new non-Albicans Candida species that pose diagnostic and therapeutic problems in critically ill neonates. Candida viswanathii is an uncommon pathogen with poor clinical evidence, particularly in neonatal critical care units. Methods From April to August 2025, we conducted a case series of five newborns admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) of Bambino Gesù Children's Hospital in Rome, Italy, who had bloodstream infections caused by C. viswanathii . Whole-genome sequencing (WGS), chromogenic agar evaluation, MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, and traditional culture were all used in microbiological identification. Broth microdilution was used to test for antifungal susceptibility. Retrospective clinical data on risk factors, treatment, and results were collected. Results Six cases of candidemia were reported in five critically unwell newborns, the majority of whom were premature or had severe congenital comorbidities. All of the patients had central venous catheters and had been in intensive care for an extended period of time. Initial identification methods misidentified isolates as Candida tropicalis , however molecular research revealed a clonal cluster of C. viswanathii . The BCID2 panel failed to detect the organism. All isolates had higher fluconazole minimum inhibitory concentrations, but echinocandins and amphotericin B had lower MIC values. Systemic echinocandin therapy was the primary treatment, with liposomal amphotericin B added in severe instances, as well as rigorous source control measures such as catheter removal and antifungal lock therapy. Microbiological clearance was documented in all six candidemia episodes. Three patients were discharged, whereas two died because of their underlying cardiopulmonary disease. Conclusions Invasive C. viswanathii infection represents a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge in the NICU. Advanced microbiological techniques, prompt source control, and targeted antifungal therapy are essential for effective management of this emerging pathogen.

title: Evaluation of Cardiac Manifestations in Acute Haemorrhagic Stroke Patients
authors: S M Abdul Awal; Biswojit Mondal; Prosad Kumer Sarker; Abul Bashar Md Mahbubul Haque
abstract: Introduction: Stroke remains a major cause of death, disability and socioeconomic burden worldwide. Although neurological injury is the primary clinical concern, acute haemorrhagic stroke can also produce important cardiovascular manifestations through autonomic dysfunction, catecholamine excess, pre-existing cardiovascular disease and direct neurocardiac interactions. These abnormalities may include electrocardiographic changes, arrhythmias, myocardial injury, left ventricular dysfunction and structural cardiac abnormalities. Early recognition may therefore assist risk stratification and clinical management. Objective: To evaluate the cardiac manifestations and associated risk factors in acute haemorrhagic stroke patients. Methods: This prospective cross-sectional observational study was conducted in the Departments of Medicine and Neurology, Khulna Medical College Hospital. A total of 50 patients with acute haemorrhagic stroke were included. Electrocardiography and two-dimensional echocardiography were performed within 24 hours of hospital admission. Demographic characteristics, vascular risk factors, ECG abnormalities, echocardiographic abnormalities and in-hospital outcomes were evaluated. Results: The mean age of the participants was 62.05 ± 9.87 years, with male-to-female ratio of 1.77:1. ECG abnormalities were identified in 74.0% of patients and echocardiographic abnormalities in 58.0%. QTc prolongation was the most frequent ECG abnormality (46.0%), followed by ST-segment depression (40.0%), U waves (32.0%), T-wave inversion (32.0%) and electrocardiographic left ventricular hypertrophy (30.0%). Echocardiography showed diastolic dysfunction in 48.0%, left ventricular hypertrophy in 36.0%, mitral regurgitation in 24.0%, aortic valve calcification in 22.0%, regional wall-motion abnormality in 12.0%, left ventricular systolic dysfunction in 10.0%, aortic regurgitation in 8.0% and left ventricular dilatation in 6.0%. Conclusion: Cardiac abnormalities were highly prevalent among patients admitted with acute haemorrhagic stroke. Early ECG assessment and echocardiography may therefore provide clinically useful information for identifying high-risk haemorrhagic-stroke patients. Medicine Today 2026, Vol.38 (2): 232-236

title: Electronic Health Record-Based Machine-Learning for Cardiac Arrhythmia Identification in Adults with High-Risk Chronic Disease: Model Development and Validation Study
authors: Mansi Goel; Shelby Matlock; Yasmin Karasu Benyes; Nanthini Narayanan; Jeremy Howard; Thomas George Brazeal; Colin Cogan; Eric Navarro; Andrei Petruș
abstract: Background: Cardiac arrhythmias may remain unrecognized in adults with chronic disease. Established risk scores primarily address atrial fibrillation. Objective: To develop and internally evaluate an electronic health record (EHR)-based machine-learning model to identify patients more likely to receive a documented cardiac arrhythmia diagnosis. Methods: We retrospectively evaluated EHR data (2018-2025) from one healthcare organization among adults with type 2 diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic kidney disease, or coronary artery disease. Logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost were compared. XGBoost was selected using internal validation, reduced to 30 features using Shapley additive explanations, and evaluated in a holdout set with data ending one day before the index date. Sensitivity analyses excluded information recorded within 30, 90, or 180 days before the index date. An atrial fibrillation/flutter-specific analysis compared XGBoost with CHARGE-AF and HARMS2-AF. Results: Among 30,356 patients, 6,835 (22.5%) had a qualifying arrhythmia diagnosis. In 3,051 holdout patients, XGBoost achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.894 (95% CI 0.879-0.908) and an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.792 (95% CI 0.763-0.822). At a 0.5 threshold, sensitivity was 0.564, specificity 0.971, and precision 0.857. AUROC remained 0.896-0.897 across earlier cutoffs. In the common score-calculable atrial fibrillation/flutter subset (n = 2,436), AUROCs were 0.883 for XGBoost, 0.712 for CHARGE-AF, and 0.554 for HARMS2-AF. Conclusions: XGBoost demonstrated strong internal discrimination for documented arrhythmias. External validation and prospective evaluation are needed to assess generalizability and clinical utility.

title: Global thickness for accurate and precise evaluation of post-intervention remodelling in left ventricular hypertrophy
authors: Lynn Khor; Hunain Shiwani; George D. Thornton; Jonathan Bennett; Nikoo Aziminia; Abhishek M. Shetye; Constantin-Cristian Topriceanu; Gabriella Captur; Rhodri Huw Davies; J C Moon; Peter Swoboda; Calvin Chin; Thomas Alexander Treibel; Rebecca Kozor; Martin Ugander
abstract: Background: Cardiovascular interventions may impact both left ventricular mass (LVM) and end-diastolic volume (EDV), but the net effect on wall thickness has been difficult to accurately evaluate. Global average left ventricular end-diastolic wall thickness (GT) relates non-linearly to LVM and EDV. We hypothesized that if GT is independent of EDV in health, then GT will be an ideal measure of post-intervention change in left ventricular hypertrophy. Methods: GT [mm] was calculated using LVM and EDV by cardiovascular magnetic resonance as previously validated. The correlation between GT and EDV was evaluated in healthy volunteers. Change in GT following intervention was evaluated for aortic stenosis undergoing valve replacement, hypertension commencing antihypertensive medications, athletes undergoing forced detraining, and aortic regurgitation undergoing valve replacement. The performance of GT was compared to LVM/EDV. Results: Among healthy volunteers (n=4461, mean+/-SD age 59+/-10 years, 50% female), EDV correlated with LVM/EDV but negligibly with GT (R2>0.16 vs R2<0.02, p<0.001 for both sexes). GT and not LVM/EDV changed after intervention in all conditions (p≤0.02 for all). Post-intervention changes in GT varied by condition (mean+/-SEM aortic stenosis [n=102]: -1.75+/-0.13mm, hypertension [n=78]: -0.66+/-0.08mm, athletes [n=28]: -0.29+/-0.09mm, aortic regurgitation [n=58]: +0.50+/-0.11 mm, p≤0.02 for all comparisons). Conclusions: In health, GT, unlike LVM/EDV, remains effectively unchanged across EDV values, indicating that GT is a physiological constant in health and can track pathological changes. After intervention, only GT and not LVM/EDV consistently changed. Instead of LVM/EDV, GT should be used to quantify remodelling after interventions in left ventricular hypertrophy.

title: High-Resolution Analysis With Multiphase Computed Tomography of the Left Atrio-Ventricular Junction in Mitral Annular Disjunction
authors: Jérôme Jouan; Damian O. Craiem; Cyrille Boulogne; Gilles Soulat; Élie Mousseaux
journal: Journal of the Heart Valve Society
abstract: Objective Among myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD), mitral annular disjunction (MAD) is associated with severe mitral regurgitation (MR). However, functional analyses are lacking to fully understand the mechanisms leading to bileaflet prolapse in MAD. Using multiphase cardiac computed tomography imaging (4D-MCCTI), we aim to characterize left atrio-ventricular junction morphological alterations throughout the cardiac cycle in patients with MAD. Methods Imaging datasets were obtained via 4D-MCCTI for 2 groups of consecutive patients with severe MR due to MMVD: 22 with MAD (MMVD + MAD+) and 20 without (MMVD + MAD−). A control group of 30 patients (MMVD−) was also included. Semi-automated delineation of 18 points around the mitral annulus (MA) allowed 3D calculation of areas, perimeters, 360°-diameters, and planar/vertical deformation across time. Left ventricular (LV) and atrial (LA) inner contours were also delineated, and systolic shortening distances from the annulus to the anterior and posterior papillary muscles (MA-APM and MA-PPM) were estimated. Results Groups were comparable for age, pulmonary pressures, and LV ejection fraction. In MMVD + MAD+, MA expansion began earlier in systole, following LA expansion, and peaking at end-systole: 3D-area: 10.9±3.7cm 2 /m 2 , compared to 8.9±2.4 cm 2 /m 2 for MMVD + MAD− ( P < .001) and 6.1±1.3 cm 2 /m 2 for MMVD− ( P < .001). However, MA perimeter reduction remained unaltered in MMVD + MAD + patients (−14.7±5.2%). In systole, MA-APM and MA-PPM reduction were greater in MMVD + MAD+: −6.58±1.99 mm, −8.12±1.26 mm versus −2.53±2.01 mm, −3.25±2.31 mm in MMVD− and −2.18±1.79 mm, −3.86±2.77 mm in MMVD + MAD− ( P < .001). Conclusions In MAD, MA becomes desynchronized from LV function. The extent of systolic MA deformation and papillary muscle movement may promote bileaflet prolapse.
